Action Name: Adopt New Energy-Efficient Building Standards for Residential Buildings
Description: Adopt mandatory guidelines for energy-efficient construction of new residential buildings, covering insulation, passive cooling design, and reflective materials. These standards reduce indoor heat exposure and lower cooling energy demand, directly mitigating heat-related health risks for occupants.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Low-income households in thermally inefficient buildings face disproportionate indoor heat exposure; standards must be applied consistently with targeted support for affordable housing.
Dependencies: Regulatory framework to enforce building standards, "Availability of sustainable building materials", "Training and education for builders and architects on energy-efficient practices", "Incentives for developers to adopt green building practices", "Monitoring and evaluation mechanisms to assess compliance with standards"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Energy consumption reduction, "Carbon emissions reduction", "Percentage of buildings meeting standards", "Cost savings from energy efficiency", "Water usage reduction", "Sustainable materials usage", "Occupant satisfaction", "Compliance rate with building standards"
Further Resources: IEA (2023). Buildings – Energy System Analysis. https://www.iea.org/energy-system/buildings | IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch9 (2022). Buildings. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-9/

Action Name: Adopt New Energy-Efficient Building Standards for Institutional Buildings
Description: Adopt mandatory guidelines for energy-efficient construction of new institutional buildings (schools, hospitals, government facilities), including passive cooling, reflective surfaces, and natural ventilation requirements. These standards reduce indoor heat stress, lower cooling energy demand, and ensure public buildings remain safe during heatwaves.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Institutional buildings are critical cooling anchors for vulnerable populations who rely on schools, clinics, and social services during extreme heat events.
Dependencies: Compliance from construction companies with the new standards, "Support from government agencies for enforcement and monitoring", "Availability of training programs for builders and architects on energy-efficient practices", "Public awareness and acceptance of sustainable building practices", "Access to funding or incentives for implementing energy-efficient technologies"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Energy consumption reduction, "Carbon emissions reduction", "Percentage of buildings meeting new standards", "Cost savings from energy efficiency", "Water usage reduction", "Sustainable materials usage", "Building occupancy rates", "Compliance rate with building codes", "Reduction in urban heat island effect", "Feedback from building occupants on comfort and sustainability"
Further Resources: IEA (2023). Buildings – Energy System Analysis. https://www.iea.org/energy-system/buildings | IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch9 (2022). Buildings. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-9/

Action Name: Enforce Energy Performance Standards for Existing Residential Buildings
Description: Enforce standards for retrofitting existing residential buildings to improve thermal performance, including better insulation, reflective roofing, natural ventilation, and energy-efficient cooling systems. Retrofits reduce indoor heat exposure and lower cooling energy costs, with particular benefits for low-income households.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Retrofit programs should prioritize low-income and informal settlement housing, where indoor heat burden is greatest and self-funding capacity is lowest.
Dependencies: Availability of funding for retrofitting and upgrades, "Access to skilled labor for implementing building improvements", "Compliance with local building codes and regulations", "Availability of energy-efficient technologies and materials", "Support from local government and stakeholders for policy implementation", "Public awareness and acceptance of sustainability practices"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Energy consumption reduction, "Greenhouse gas emissions reduction", "Percentage of buildings meeting new standards", "Cost savings from energy efficiency improvements", "Increase in renewable energy usage", "Occupant satisfaction and comfort levels", "Reduction in water usage", "Improvement in indoor air quality", "Rate of retrofitted buildings", "Time taken for compliance with standards"
Further Resources: C40 Knowledge Hub (2022). Existing Building Standards Action Guide. https://www.c40knowledgehub.org | IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch9 (2022). Buildings. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-9/

Action Name: Enforce Energy Performance Standards for Existing Commercial Buildings
Description: Enforce standards for improving the energy and thermal performance of existing commercial buildings through retrofits—covering upgrades to insulation, windows, roofing, and HVAC systems. These measures reduce building heat gain and occupant heat stress during extreme heat events.
Subsector: commercial and institutional buildings and facilities
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Retrofits should improve working conditions for employees in hot environments; support programs must be accessible to small businesses and informal employers.
Dependencies: Availability of funding and financial incentives for building upgrades, "Access to skilled labor and contractors for implementing improvements", "Compliance with local building codes and regulations", "Availability of technology and materials for energy-efficient upgrades", "Engagement and support from building owners and tenants", "Data on current building performance and energy usage for assessment"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Energy consumption reduction, "Greenhouse gas emissions reduction", "Percentage of buildings meeting energy efficiency standards", "Cost savings from energy efficiency improvements", "Increase in renewable energy usage", "Occupant satisfaction and comfort levels", "Retrofit completion rate", "Water usage reduction", "Building certification levels (e.g., LEED, BREEAM)", "Reduction in operational costs"
Further Resources: C40 Knowledge Hub (2022). Existing Building Standards Action Guide. https://www.c40knowledgehub.org | IEA (2023). Buildings – Energy System Analysis. https://www.iea.org/energy-system/buildings

Action Name: Develop District Heating and Cooling Networks
Description: Develop shared infrastructure to distribute thermally conditioned water to multiple buildings, enabling efficient cooling at scale. District cooling systems reduce the urban heat island effect compared to individual air conditioning units and provide cost-effective access to cooling in dense urban areas.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: District cooling must use inclusive pricing models to serve dense urban areas where individual air conditioning is unaffordable for low-income residents.
Dependencies: Investment in infrastructure to build and maintain heat networks, "Collaboration with local government and stakeholders for planning and implementation", "Access to renewable energy sources to supply heat", "Public awareness and acceptance of heat networks", "Regulatory frameworks that support energy efficiency and sustainability initiatives"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Reduction in carbon emissions (tons/year), "Energy efficiency improvement (% increase)", "Percentage of buildings connected to heat networks (%)", "Cost savings for consumers ($/year)", "Heat loss reduction in distribution system (% decrease)", "Increase in renewable energy sources used (%)", "User satisfaction rate (%)", "Operational reliability of heat networks (% uptime)", "Investment in infrastructure ($)", "Reduction in energy consumption (MWh/year)"
Further Resources: IEA (2022). District Heating. https://www.iea.org/energy-system/buildings/district-heating | UNEP (2021). District Energy in Cities Initiative. https://www.unep.org/explore-topics/energy/what-we-do/district-energy-cities

Action Name: Promote Net-Zero and Green Building Certifications
Description: Promote sustainable buildings by supporting net-zero energy goals and encouraging green building certifications such as LEED. It aims to incentivize the construction and renovation of buildings that produce as much energy as they consume, reducing their environmental impact. This initiative also fosters the adoption of sustainable practices and technologies, ensuring long-term energy efficiency and environmental responsibility across residential, commercial, and public infrastructure.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Certification pathways must include social housing and affordable buildings; low-income residents face greatest heat exposure but have least capacity to self-fund upgrades.
Dependencies: Availability of financial incentives, subsidies, or tax credits to encourage homeowners to install solar, wind, and other clean energy systems, "Access to information and educational resources to help homeowners understand the benefits, costs, and installation processes for clean energy systems", "Development of supportive regulations and policies that facilitate the installation of renewable energy technologies in residential areas"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of buildings certified as net-zero or green buildings annually., "Reduction in energy and water consumption in certified buildings (kWh/year, m³/year).", "Estimated reduction in CO₂ equivalent emissions from green building practices."
Further Resources: US Green Building Council. LEED Certification. https://www.usgbc.org/leed | C40 Knowledge Hub. Net-Zero Building Standards. https://www.c40knowledgehub.org

Action Name: Create a Financial Support Program for Extreme Weather Event Response
Description: Create a dedicated financial support program to assist households, businesses, and communities affected by extreme weather events including heatwaves, floods, and droughts. The program should prioritize recovery for the most vulnerable populations and support investment in heat-resilient rebuilding.
Hazard Name: Extreme Heat, Droughts, Diseases, Landslides, Wildfires, Floods, Sea Level Rise, Storms
Sector: Emergency management; Public Health; Economic Development; City Administration
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Programs must prioritize informal settlements and low-income households with highest exposure and fewest financial reserves; simple, multilingual applications are essential.
Dependencies: Financial resources, "Emergency response plans", "Institutional coordination"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of people assisted, "Cost-effectiveness", "Community resilience"
Further Resources: IPCC AR6 WGII Ch8 (2022). Poverty, Livelihoods and Sustainable Development. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-8/ | World Bank (2022). Investing in People to Fight Poverty and Boost Shared Prosperity. https://www.worldbank.org

Action Name: Expand Urban Biodiversity through Nature-Based Solutions
Description: Expand and restore diverse urban ecosystems—including green corridors, wetlands, and urban forests—to reduce urban heat island intensity through evapotranspiration and shading. These nature-based solutions deliver co-benefits for biodiversity, stormwater management, and community wellbeing.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Green spaces must be distributed equitably across the city, prioritizing low-income neighborhoods historically underserved in environmental amenities and facing higher heat exposure.
Dependencies: Availability of funding for green space projects, "Community engagement and support for biodiversity initiatives", "Collaboration with local governments and environmental organizations", "Access to scientific research on local ecosystems", "Regulatory frameworks that support land conservation and urban planning"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Increase in green space area (hectares), "Number of native species introduced", "Biodiversity index improvement", "Percentage of urban areas with accessible green spaces", "Community engagement in biodiversity programs", "Reduction in urban heat island effect", "Increase in pollinator populations", "Improvement in air quality metrics", "Number of partnerships with local conservation organizations", "Public awareness and education outreach metrics"
Further Resources: C40 Knowledge Hub. Biodiversity Expansion Action Guide. https://www.c40knowledgehub.org | IPCC AR6 WGII Ch2 (2022). Terrestrial and Freshwater Ecosystems and Their Services. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-2/

Action Name: Deploy a Heat Early Warning and Hydrometeorological Monitoring System
Description: Deploy heat early warning and hydrometeorological monitoring systems to detect and communicate forecasted dangerous heat conditions, enabling proactive emergency response. Integrate real-time temperature and humidity monitoring with targeted alerts to health authorities, emergency services, and the public to significantly reduce heat-related mortality.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Early warning systems must reach elderly, chronically ill, and informal settlement residents via multi-channel, multilingual outreach—SMS, community radio, and door-to-door contact.
Dependencies: Access to reliable climate data and forecasting models, "Effective communication infrastructure for disseminating warnings", "Community engagement and education on climate risks", "Collaboration with local and national emergency response agencies", "Funding and resources for technology and system maintenance"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of early warnings issued, "Response time to warnings", "Levels of community awareness and preparedness", "Reduction of disaster-related damage", "Number of training sessions held", "Stakeholder engagement and participation rates", "Community feedback on effectiveness of warnings", "Frequency of exercises and drills conducted", "Reduction in heatwave-related death rates", "Timeliness of Warnings"
Further Resources: WHO (2021). Heat-Health Action Plans. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240008410 | WMO (2022). Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems: A Checklist. https://library.wmo.int/doc_num.php?explnum_id=11126

Action Name: Reform Urban Form to Reduce Heat Exposure and Carbon Emissions
Description: Reform urban spatial form by increasing density, mixing land uses, and designing for walkability to reduce car dependency, commuting heat exposure, and urban heat island intensity. Compact, connected urban form also reduces energy consumption in buildings and transport.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Improves access to affordable, efficient transport for underserved communities, reducing social and economic disparities linked to car dependency and heat exposure.
Dependencies: Policy support for land-use planning, "public acceptance", "reallocation of transport budgets towards sustainable modes"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Reduction in per capita car use, "increase in public transport ridership", "improved walkability index"
Further Resources: IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch8 (2022). Urban Systems and Other Settlements. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-8/ | C40 Cities (2022). State and Trends in Urban Climate Action. https://www.c40.org

Action Name: Restore and Expand Forest and Degraded Ecosystems through Afforestation
Description: Restore degraded forest ecosystems through large-scale afforestation and reforestation programs in urban and peri-urban areas. Increased tree cover reduces surface and air temperatures through shading and evapotranspiration, mitigating the urban heat island effect while sequestering carbon.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Supports local livelihoods, promotes land-use equity, and requires inclusive stakeholder participation in planning to prevent displacement of forest-dependent and low-income communities.
Dependencies: Requires funding for land restoration, "access to suitable species for planting", "local community engagement", "monitoring systems for ecosystem integrity and carbon sequestration"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Area of land reforested or afforested, "carbon sequestration rates", "improvement in biodiversity indices", "ecosystem service metrics such as water regulation and soil quality"
Further Resources: IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch7 (2022). Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Uses. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-7/ | EPA (2023). Trees and Vegetation. https://www.epa.gov/heatislands/using-trees-and-vegetation-reduce-heat-islands

Action Name: Integrate Green-Blue Infrastructure in City Projects
Description: Integrate green-blue infrastructure—combining vegetation, soil, and water features—into city planning and public works projects. Green-blue infrastructure reduces surface runoff, lowers ambient temperatures through evapotranspiration, and improves urban biodiversity and wellbeing.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Investments must prioritize low-income areas lacking cooling green space, with community participation to prevent gentrification and displacement of residents most at risk.
Dependencies: Development of integrated water and green area policies to align urban water management with green infrastructure goals., "Availability of technical expertise and funding to implement blue infrastructure projects, such as sustainable drainage systems and water retention areas.", "Collaboration with urban planners, environmental organizations, and local governments to design and manage blue infrastructure that supports ecosystem restoration and climate resilience."
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Increase in water retention capacity of urban areas (m³)., "Reduction in urban flooding incidents post-implementation (%).", "Increase in green spaces linked to water features (hectares)."
Further Resources: IUCN (2020). Global Standard for Nature-based Solutions. https://portals.iucn.org/library/node/49070 | C40 Knowledge Hub. Green-Blue Infrastructure Action Guide. https://www.c40knowledgehub.org

Action Name: Install Permeable Pavements
Description: Install permeable and semi-permeable pavements in streets, parking areas, and public spaces to enable stormwater infiltration and evaporative cooling. Combine with nature-based solutions such as bioswales and green strips to lower ambient temperatures and manage urban flooding.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Prioritize low-income neighborhoods and informal settlements with highest impervious coverage and heat-flood risk; local employment in installation extends social benefits.
Dependencies: Expansion of permeable and semi-permeable areas in City-administered buildings and public spaces., "Adoption of nature-based solutions (NbS) such as urban tree planting, green roofs, rainwater cisterns, and bio-swales.", "Feasibility analyses for permeable pavements and increased green areas in roadways, alongside traditional stormwater management solutions like curbs, gutters, and retention ponds."
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Reduction in surface water runoff during rainfall events (%)., "Decrease in flooding occurrences in modified areas.", "Percentage of public spaces complying with new permeable surface regulations."
Further Resources: EPA (2021). Soak Up the Rain: Permeable Pavement. https://www.epa.gov/soakuptherain/soak-rain-permeable-pavement | Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Cool Pavements. https://heatisland.lbl.gov/coolscience/cool-pavements

Action Name: Retrofit Urban Infrastructure for Climate and Heat Resilience
Description: Retrofit existing urban infrastructure—including roads, bridges, utilities, and public spaces—to withstand increased heat, flooding, and other climate hazards. Upgrades include heat-resistant materials, improved drainage, and enhanced thermal performance.
Sector: Road infrastructure; Public Health; Energy Security
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Improves resilience for vulnerable communities, especially those in low-income areas, by reducing infrastructure risks from extreme heat and climate change.
Dependencies: Policy alignment, "Funding availability", "Engineering and construction expertise"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Reduced infrastructure failure during hazards, "Increased capacity for housing and energy systems"
Further Resources: IPCC AR6 WGII Ch6 (2022). Cities, Settlements and Key Infrastructure. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-6/ | UNDRR (2023). Infrastructure and Disaster Risk. https://www.undrr.org

Action Name: Incorporate Natural Shading and Ventilation in Building Design
Description: Encourage the use of architectural features such as shaded facades, green roofs, and cross-ventilation to reduce reliance on mechanical cooling systems.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Passive cooling is most valuable for low-income households who cannot afford air conditioning; building codes should specifically address social housing and informal settlements.
Dependencies: Development of building design guidelines and standards that promote the integration of passive cooling features like shaded facades, green roofs, and cross-ventilation, "Availability of financial incentives or support for incorporating energy-efficient architectural features in both new and existing buildings", "Collaboration with architects, urban planners, and local authorities to integrate these features into urban development and renovation projects"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of buildings incorporating natural shading/ventilation., "Reduction in cooling energy demand (%) per building.", "Temperature resilience improvements in monitored buildings (°C)."
Further Resources: ASHRAE (2022). Standard 55-2020: Thermal Environmental Conditions for Human Occupancy. https://www.ashrae.org | IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch9 (2022). Buildings. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-9/

Action Name: Encourage Energy and Thermal Benchmarking in Buildings
Description: Encourage the comparison of energy performance in public buildings.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Benchmarking must support small landlords and social housing operators with limited capacity; public results help low-income tenants advocate for thermal improvements.
Dependencies: Establish standardized metrics and a transparent reporting system for energy performance., "Provide training for facility managers on energy efficiency.", "Offer incentives to encourage energy performance improvements in public buildings."
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of buildings that perform energy benchmarking annually., "Percentage reduction in the average energy consumption of monitored buildings (%).", "Energy savings achieved in participating buildings (kWh/year)."
Further Resources: ASHRAE (2022). Building Energy Benchmarking Guidance. https://www.ashrae.org | EPA ENERGY STAR (2023). Portfolio Manager. https://www.energystar.gov/buildings/facility-owners-and-managers/existing-buildings/use-portfolio-manager

Action Name: Install Public Shading Structures in Urban Spaces
Description: Install shade structures in public spaces—including canopies, pergolas, tree canopy, and covered transit stops—to reduce radiant and ambient heat exposure for pedestrians. Shading can reduce perceived temperature by 10–15°C in outdoor spaces and is particularly effective at protecting vulnerable populations during heatwaves.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Shading most benefits elderly, children, low-income workers, and unhoused people who spend more time outdoors; prioritize underserved neighborhoods and transit corridors.
Dependencies: Availability of funding for the construction and maintenance of shade structures, "Collaboration with urban planners and architects for design integration", "Community engagement to ensure public support and usage", "Assessment of local climate conditions to determine optimal shading solutions", "Compliance with local regulations and zoning laws regarding public space modifications"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Reduction in average surface temperature in shaded areas, "Increase in public space usage during peak heat hours", "Number of shade structures installed", "User satisfaction ratings of shaded areas", "Decrease in heat-related health incidents", "Increase in biodiversity in shaded areas", "Energy savings in nearby buildings due to reduced heat", "Community engagement and participation in shading initiatives"

Action Name: Develop Urban and Community Gardens
Description: Develop urban and community gardens on underutilized or vacant land to create productive green spaces that reduce local surface temperatures through evapotranspiration, support food security, and provide community hubs for heat relief and social cohesion.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Gardens deliver greatest value in food deserts and informal settlements; inclusive governance with secure land tenure prevents appropriation by higher-income residents.
Dependencies: Ensure availability of detailed land-use maps and urban planning data., "Engage with local communities to understand their needs and expectations.", "Evaluate soil quality, water availability, and form partnerships to support the establishment and maintenance of gardens."
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of urban gardens created., "Amount of locally produced food (kg/year).", "Number of direct beneficiaries."

Action Name: Deploy Cool and Light-Colored Pavement Materials
Description: Deploy cool and light-colored pavement materials—including reflective coatings, porous asphalt, and permeable paver blocks—to reduce pavement surface temperatures by reflecting solar radiation. This lowers ambient air temperatures, extends pavement lifespan, and reduces the urban heat island effect in high-traffic areas.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Cool pavement programs should prioritize streets in low-income and informal neighborhoods with less greenery and more intense urban heat island effects.
Dependencies: Availability of reflective materials suitable for urban infrastructure, "Support from local government and urban planners for implementation", "Funding and financial resources for installation and maintenance", "Public awareness and community engagement in climate action initiatives", "Research and data on urban heat islands and their impacts"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Reduction in surface temperature of pavements, "Percentage of area covered by cool pavements", "Decrease in urban heat island effect", "Energy savings in nearby buildings", "Reduction in heat-related health incidents", "Increase in public awareness and engagement", "Cost-effectiveness of implementation", "Longevity and durability of materials used"

Action Name: Expand and Enhance Parks and Public Green Spaces
Description: Expand urban green spaces and parks across all neighborhoods, prioritizing heat-exposed and underserved areas, to reduce urban heat island intensity, improve air quality, and enhance community wellbeing.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Expansion must prioritize low-income communities with least existing canopy, addressing the strong historical correlation between neighborhood income and access to cooling vegetation.
Dependencies: Availability of land for park development and expansion, "Funding for park construction and ongoing maintenance", "Community engagement and support for green space initiatives", "Collaboration with urban planners and local government", "Regulatory frameworks supporting green space requirements in underserved areas"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Increase in green space area per capita (m²/person), "Number of new parks and green spaces created", "Percentage of population within 300m of accessible green space", "Reduction in ambient temperature in expanded green areas (°C)", "Reduction in urban heat island intensity in target neighborhoods"
Further Resources: EPA (2023). Using Trees and Vegetation to Reduce Heat Islands. https://www.epa.gov/heatislands | C40 Knowledge Hub. Urban Forests Action Guide. https://www.c40knowledgehub.org

Action Name: Improve Building Envelopes with Heat-Resilient Materials
Description: Improve building envelopes using heat-resilient materials and construction techniques—including high-performance insulation, reflective cladding, and thermally massive walls—to reduce heat gain in summer and lower cooling energy requirements.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Prioritize low-income households facing highest indoor heat burden; subsidies and financing are critical to ensure envelope upgrades reach those with fewest resources.
Dependencies: Availability of heat-resilient building materials in local markets, "Regulatory standards for thermal performance of building envelopes", "Training and certification programs for contractors and builders", "Financial incentives or subsidies for building envelope upgrades", "Building code enforcement mechanisms"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of buildings upgraded with heat-resilient envelope materials, "Reduction in cooling energy demand per building (%)", "Average reduction in indoor temperature during heat events (°C)", "Energy savings achieved in upgraded buildings (kWh/year)", "Percentage of buildings compliant with thermal performance standards"
Further Resources: ASHRAE (2022). Standard 90.1-2022: Energy Standard for Buildings. https://www.ashrae.org | EPA (2023). Heat Island Effect: Buildings. https://www.epa.gov/heatislands

Action Name: Train Building Operators in Energy and Heat Management
Description: Train building operators and facility managers in energy management, HVAC optimization, and heat emergency protocols to improve building performance during heat events and reduce energy consumption.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Training should target operators in social housing and affordable buildings where low-income residents face high heat risk and benefit most from improved management.
Dependencies: Development of training curriculum and certification programs for building operators, "Availability of qualified trainers and instructors", "Funding for training programs and facilities", "Engagement and commitment from building owners and facility managers", "Collaboration with industry associations and government agencies"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of building operators trained, "Reduction in energy consumption in participating buildings (%)", "Number of buildings with certified heat management operators", "Improvement in HVAC system efficiency ratings", "Reduction in heat-related incidents in managed buildings"
Further Resources: ASHRAE (2022). Building Operator Certification. https://www.ashrae.org | IEA (2023). Buildings – Energy System Analysis. https://www.iea.org/energy-system/buildings

Action Name: Establish Community Cooling Centers for Heat Emergency Relief
Description: Establish designated community cooling centers—such as libraries, community halls, and transit stations—that provide free, accessible refuge from extreme heat for vulnerable residents who lack home cooling, with extended hours during heat emergencies.
Sector: Disaster Risk Management; Public Health; Education; Transportation; Informal Settlements
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Site cooling centers to minimize transportation barriers for elderly, low-income, and disabled populations; prioritize underserved neighborhoods with highest heat vulnerability.
Dependencies: Identification and designation of suitable facilities as cooling centers, "Funding for operations, cooling equipment, and staffing", "Community awareness campaigns on cooling center locations and hours", "Coordination with health and emergency services", "Protocols for extended hours and activation during heat emergencies"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of cooling centers established and operational, "Number of people served during heat emergencies", "Geographic coverage of cooling centers (% of population within access distance)", "Reduction in heat-related hospitalizations in served areas", "Average response time for opening centers during declared heat emergencies"
Further Resources: CDC (2023). Cooling Centers. https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/emres/heat.html | WHO (2021). Heat-Health Action Plans. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240008410

Action Name: Install Cooling Systems in Transit Stations
Description: Install cooling and ventilation systems in transit stations and bus shelters to provide thermal comfort for commuters during extreme heat events, making public transit a more viable and safe option during heatwaves.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Prioritize cooling installations on corridors and stations serving heat-vulnerable, low-income neighborhoods to provide thermal relief for transit-dependent and outdoor commuters.
Dependencies: Infrastructure assessment of transit stations for cooling system feasibility, "Capital funding for cooling system installation", "Collaboration with transit authorities and operators", "Adequate energy supply infrastructure for cooling systems", "Maintenance protocols and technical expertise for system operations"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of transit stations with cooling systems installed, "Reduction in platform temperature during peak heat events (°C)", "Increase in public transit ridership during heatwave periods (%)", "Energy consumption of installed cooling systems (kWh/year)", "User satisfaction ratings in cooled transit stations"

Action Name: Aggregate Cooling Demand to Improve Energy Efficiency
Description: Aggregate cooling demand from multiple buildings to negotiate lower prices, enable shared infrastructure, and improve overall system efficiency, reducing the energy and cost burden of cooling during extreme heat events.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Aggregated programs should include social housing and affordable buildings to ensure efficiency benefits reach low-income residents, not only large commercial users.
Dependencies: Formation of building owner cooperatives or demand aggregation consortia, "Shared metering and monitoring infrastructure across participating buildings", "Regulatory frameworks or utility agreements supporting demand aggregation", "Technical expertise for demand management and negotiation", "Engagement and commitment from participating building owners"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Reduction in aggregated cooling energy consumption (%), "Cost savings from demand aggregation for participating buildings ($/year)", "Number of buildings participating in aggregation programs", "Peak demand reduction during heat events (kW)", "Reduction in carbon emissions from cooling (tons CO₂/year)"
Further Resources: IEA (2023). Smart Grids. https://www.iea.org/energy-system/electricity/smart-grids | UNEP (2022). Cooling Emissions and Policy Synthesis Report. https://www.unep.org

Action Name: Install Green Roofs to Reduce Urban Heat
Description: Install vegetated roofs on buildings to reduce rooftop surface temperatures through evapotranspiration and insulation, lower cooling energy demand, manage stormwater, and provide urban biodiversity habitat.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Green roof requirements must account for affordability barriers; financial incentives and technical support are essential to include low-income and older building owners.
Dependencies: Structural assessment of buildings for green roof load-bearing suitability, "Availability of funding and financial incentives for installation", "Technical expertise for green roof installation and ongoing maintenance", "Regulatory frameworks or building codes supporting green roof requirements", "Access to appropriate plant species and growing media suited to local climate"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Total area of green roofs installed (m²), "Reduction in rooftop surface temperature (°C)", "Reduction in cooling energy demand in buildings with green roofs (%)", "Volume of stormwater retained by green roofs (m³/year)", "Increase in urban biodiversity index in green roof areas"

Action Name: Launch Public Heat Awareness and Education Campaigns
Description: Launch targeted public campaigns to raise awareness of heat risks, heat emergency symptoms, and protective behaviors, reaching vulnerable populations through multiple channels including SMS, community radio, social media, and neighborhood networks.
Sector: Disaster Risk Management; Public Health; Education; Informal Settlements
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Campaigns should target schools, senior centers, and spaces frequented by vulnerable populations; address digital access barriers by prioritizing visible, in-person communications.
Dependencies: Development of targeted communication materials for heat risks and protective behaviors, "Multi-channel communication infrastructure (SMS, radio, social media, community networks)", "Partnerships with community organizations and health agencies for outreach", "Funding for campaign development and dissemination", "Reach data and feedback mechanisms to assess campaign effectiveness"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of people reached by heat awareness campaigns, "Increase in public knowledge of heat risks and protective behaviors (%)", "Number of communication channels utilized in campaigns", "Reduction in heat-related illness and mortality rates during campaigns", "Community engagement and satisfaction ratings"
Further Resources: WHO (2021). Heat-Health Action Plans. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240008410 | Bouchama, A. et al. (2007). Prognostic factors in heat wave related deaths. Archives of Internal Medicine 167(20).

Action Name: Develop Heat-Resilient Urban Design Guidelines
Description: Develop design guidelines that embed heat resilience requirements into urban planning standards, covering building orientation, shading, green space ratios, and material specifications to create cooler, more livable cities.
Sector: Buildings; Parks; Public Works; Economic Development; Transportation
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Guidelines must ensure heat-resilient design standards apply equitably across all neighborhoods, including informal settlements and social housing, not only high-value developments.
Dependencies: Multi-disciplinary expert working group including architects, planners, and climate scientists, "Review of international best practices and local climate data", "Stakeholder consultation with government, private sector, and community", "Integration with existing urban planning legislation and regulations", "Pilot projects to test and validate design guidelines before broader adoption"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of new developments complying with heat-resilient design guidelines, "Reduction in urban heat island effect in areas applying guidelines (%)", "Number of planning applications incorporating heat resilience criteria", "Percentage of city area covered by heat-resilient design standards", "Reduction in peak outdoor temperature in guideline-compliant developments (°C)"
Further Resources: Atlantic Council Extreme Heat Resilience Alliance (2022). Heat Design Guidelines. https://www.atlanticcouncil.org | ASHRAE (2022). Standard 55: Thermal Environmental Conditions. https://www.ashrae.org

Action Name: Develop and Activate a Heat Emergency Response Plan
Description: Develop and activate a formal heat emergency response plan that defines trigger thresholds, agency responsibilities, communication protocols, and resource deployment procedures for protecting vulnerable populations during extreme heat events.
Sector: Disaster Risk Management; Public Health; Informal Settlements
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Plans must include multilingual communications and prioritize outreach to elderly, low-income, and isolated residents with highest heat risk and lowest self-protection capacity.
Dependencies: Multi-agency coordination framework with defined roles and responsibilities, "Established heat trigger thresholds linked to meteorological monitoring", "Pre-positioned resources and communication protocols for emergency activation", "Training and capacity building for all participating emergency agencies", "Regular drills and plan reviews to maintain readiness"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of heat emergencies with formally coordinated multi-agency response, "Average response time from trigger threshold to emergency activation (hours)", "Reduction in heat-related mortality during declared heat emergencies", "Percentage of target vulnerable population reached during emergency alerts", "Number of agencies trained and participating in heat response plan"
Further Resources: WHO (2021). Heat-Health Action Plans. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240008410 | CDC (2023). Extreme Heat Emergency Response. https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/emres/heat.html

Action Name: Establish Heat Hotlines for Emergency Assistance
Description: Establish and publicize dedicated heat hotlines that provide information, referrals to cooling centers, and wellness checks to residents during heatwaves, with particular outreach to elderly, isolated, and medically vulnerable populations.
Sector: Disaster Risk Management; Public Health; Informal Settlements
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Hotlines should offer multilingual support and year-round accessibility, with targeted outreach to elderly, low-income, and digitally excluded communities with highest heat vulnerability.
Dependencies: Dedicated telecommunication infrastructure and staffing for hotline operations, "Training programs for hotline operators on heat illness and service referrals", "Multi-channel publicizing of hotline numbers (media, community organizations, hospitals)", "Coordination with health services, cooling centers, and emergency responders", "Funding for ongoing operations during heat season"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of calls received during heat emergencies, "Average response time per call (minutes)", "Number of wellness checks conducted through hotline referrals", "Number of referrals to cooling centers and health services made", "Reduction in heat-related incidents among populations who contacted the hotline"
Further Resources: WHO (2021). Heat-Health Action Plans. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240008410 | Robine, J.-M. et al. (2008). Death toll exceeded 70,000 in Europe during summer 2003. Comptes Rendus Biologies.

Action Name: Integrate Heat Resilience Criteria into Environmental Impact Assessments
Description: Integrate heat resilience criteria into environmental impact assessment (EIA) frameworks, requiring that new infrastructure and development projects demonstrate they will not exacerbate urban heat and include measures to mitigate heat risks.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: EIA frameworks must require heat vulnerability assessments for low-income and informal areas, ensuring new developments do not increase risk for marginalized communities.
Dependencies: Development of standardized heat resilience criteria for EIA frameworks, "Training for EIA practitioners and regulators on heat risk assessment methods", "Legislative or regulatory mandate requiring heat criteria in EIA processes", "Collaboration with environmental agencies, urban planners, and climate scientists", "Monitoring and enforcement mechanisms to verify heat mitigation compliance"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of EIAs incorporating heat resilience criteria annually, "Percentage of new major development projects assessed for heat risk (%)", "Number of projects requiring heat mitigation measures following EIA review", "Reduction in heat vulnerability scores of approved development projects", "Quality rating of heat assessments submitted in EIA reports"
Further Resources: Atlantic Council Extreme Heat Resilience Alliance (2022). Heat-Resilient EIAs. https://www.atlanticcouncil.org | UNEP (2021). Environmental Impact Assessment Guidelines. https://www.unep.org

Action Name: Enforce Occupational Heat Safety Policies for Outdoor Workers
Description: Enforce occupational heat safety policies—including work-rest schedules, mandatory shade and water access, and heat illness training—to protect outdoor and manual workers from dangerous heat exposure during extreme heat events.
Sector: Emergency management; Public Health; Economic Development; City Administration
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Workers—especially informal, low-wage, and migrant employees—must be consulted in policy development; accountability measures must allow workers to safely report non-compliant employers.
Dependencies: Clear regulatory standards for occupational heat safety with defined thresholds, "Enforcement capacity with inspectors trained in heat safety compliance", "Employer awareness and compliance programs across high-risk sectors", "Training materials on heat illness recognition and prevention for workers", "Collaboration with labor unions, industry associations, and health agencies"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Percentage of employers complying with heat safety policies (%), "Reduction in heat-related occupational illnesses and injuries", "Number of outdoor workers receiving heat safety training", "Number of workplace heat safety inspections conducted annually", "Penalty enforcement rate for non-compliant employers"
Further Resources: ILO (2019). Working on a Warmer Planet. https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---dgreports/---dcomm/---publ/documents/publication/wcms_711919.pdf | WHO (2023). Heat and Health in Workplaces. https://www.who.int

Action Name: Establish Payments for Urban Ecosystem Services (PUES)
Description: Establish payment mechanisms that compensate landowners, communities, and institutions for maintaining urban ecosystem services—including cooling, stormwater management, and biodiversity—that benefit the broader city population.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Payment schemes must equitably distribute benefits to low-income landowners and communities managing urban green space and delivering cooling services to city residents.
Dependencies: Legal and regulatory framework enabling ecosystem service payment mechanisms, "Validated valuation methodology for urban ecosystem services", "Sustained funding sources for payment disbursements", "Engagement and agreement from landowners and community participants", "Monitoring and verification systems to assess ecosystem service delivery"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of landowners and communities receiving ecosystem service payments, "Area of urban ecosystems maintained through payment schemes (hectares)", "Estimated economic value of ecosystem services compensated annually ($/year)", "Increase in urban green and blue infrastructure maintained under payment programs", "Reduction in urban heat island intensity in areas covered by PUES agreements"
Further Resources: TEEB (2011). The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity. https://teebweb.org | C40 Knowledge Hub. Urban Ecosystem Services. https://www.c40knowledgehub.org

Action Name: Offer Property Tax Rebates for Heat-Resilient Building Upgrades
Description: Offer property tax rebates to homeowners and building owners who invest in heat-resilient building upgrades—such as cool roofs, insulation, or shading—reducing financial barriers and incentivizing uptake of heat reduction measures.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Tax rebate programs must reach low- and moderate-income homeowners, not only high-capital developers; simplified applications and pre-approval pathways ensure equitable access.
Dependencies: Legislative authority to offer property tax rebates for qualifying upgrades, "Defined eligibility criteria and verification mechanisms for heat-resilient upgrades", "Adequate municipal budget to cover rebate program costs", "Public awareness campaigns on rebate program eligibility and application process", "Coordination with building assessment and tax collection authorities"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of property owners receiving heat-resilient upgrade tax rebates, "Total value of tax rebates distributed annually ($)", "Number of heat-resilient upgrades completed with rebate support", "Reduction in cooling energy consumption in participating properties (%)", "Uptake rate of heat-resilient technologies in rebate-eligible properties"
Further Resources: ACEEE (2022). Financing Energy Efficiency. https://www.aceee.org | C40 Knowledge Hub. Building Retrofit Financing. https://www.c40knowledgehub.org

Action Name: Maintain and Expand Public Transit Services during Heatwaves
Description: Maintain and expand public transit services specifically during heat emergencies, including extended operating hours and free fares, to provide access to cooling centers for residents without private transport and reduce dangerous outdoor exposure.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Targeted outreach ensures low-income and transit-dependent communities know about expanded services; cooling centers must be located near accessible transit for vulnerable users.
Dependencies: Coordination agreements with transit authorities and operators for emergency service expansion, "Funding for extended services and free fare periods during heat emergencies", "Heat emergency trigger criteria linked to transit service activation plans", "Communication infrastructure to publicize service changes to the public", "Adequate cooled transit vehicles and infrastructure to support expanded services"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of additional transit trips provided during heat emergencies, "Increase in transit ridership during declared heatwave events (%)", "Percentage of transit routes with extended hours during heat emergencies", "Number of people accessing cooling centers via expanded public transit", "Reduction in outdoor heat exposure incidents linked to transport access"
Further Resources: UITP (2021). Public Transport and Climate Change. https://www.uitp.org | WHO (2021). Heat-Health Action Plans. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240008410

Action Name: Install Public Water Features for Urban Cooling
Description: Install public water features—including fountains, misting stations, and splash pads—in high-traffic public spaces to provide evaporative cooling and accessible heat relief for pedestrians and outdoor workers during heatwaves.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Water features should be sited in heat-exposed, low-income public spaces, prioritizing areas where residents lack access to private cooling alternatives.
Dependencies: Identification and assessment of high-traffic public locations for water feature installation, "Funding for construction, water supply, and ongoing maintenance", "Water supply infrastructure and management capacity", "Community engagement to ensure public acceptance and usage", "Technical expertise for installation, operation, and maintenance"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of public water features installed, "Reduction in ambient temperature at installation sites (°C)", "Number of people using water features during peak heat events", "Reduction in heat-related illness in target public areas", "User satisfaction ratings for water features"
Further Resources: C40 Knowledge Hub. Water Features for Urban Cooling. https://www.c40knowledgehub.org | EPA (2023). Heat Island Cooling Strategies. https://www.epa.gov/heatislands/heat-island-cooling-strategies

Action Name: Replace Impervious Surfaces to Reduce Urban Heat and Runoff
Description: Replace impervious paved surfaces with permeable alternatives, green space, or reflective materials to reduce heat absorption, enable evaporative cooling, and decrease stormwater runoff in urban areas.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Prioritize impervious surface replacement in low-income and informal neighborhoods bearing the highest combined heat and flood burden from excessive surface sealing.
Dependencies: Mapping and prioritization of impervious surface areas for replacement, "Funding for surface replacement and installation works", "Availability of permeable, green, or reflective replacement materials", "Technical expertise for installation and long-term maintenance", "Integration with urban stormwater management and drainage planning"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Area of impervious surfaces replaced with permeable or reflective alternatives (m²), "Reduction in urban surface temperature in modified areas (°C)", "Decrease in stormwater runoff volume post-implementation (%)", "Reduction in urban heat island intensity in target areas", "Increase in permeable surface ratio across urban areas (%)"
Further Resources: EPA (2021). Soak Up the Rain: Permeable Pavement. https://www.epa.gov/soakuptherain | LBNL. Cool Pavements. https://heatisland.lbl.gov/coolscience/cool-pavements

Action Name: Support Access to Efficient Residential Air Conditioning With Clean Energy
Description: Support access to efficient, affordable residential air conditioning for low-income and heat-vulnerable households through subsidy programs, equipment lending, and financial assistance, while promoting energy-efficient technologies to limit electricity demand growth.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Prioritize low-income and heat-vulnerable households; pair AC support with clean energy options and weatherization to prevent increased emissions and energy bill burdens.
Dependencies: Availability of targeted financial subsidies and assistance programs for vulnerable households, "Market availability of energy-efficient and affordable cooling technologies", "Coordination with energy utilities for clean energy supply integration", "Outreach and enrollment support for heat-vulnerable and low-income households", "Energy efficiency standards and certification criteria for eligible equipment"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of heat-vulnerable households receiving residential AC support, "Average energy efficiency rating of installed cooling systems", "Reduction in heat-related illness among supported households", "Increase in proportion of residential cooling powered by clean energy (%)", "Average cost savings for supported households ($/year)"
Further Resources: IEA (2023). Cooling. https://www.iea.org/energy-system/buildings/cooling | UNEP (2022). Cooling Emissions and Policy Synthesis Report. https://www.unep.org

Action Name: Plant Street Trees to Create Cool Corridors and Provide Shading and Cooling
Description: Implement a systematic street-tree planting program to create continuous "cool corridors" along transit routes, sidewalks, and residential streets. This action targets the reduction of the Urban Heat Island effect by shading heat-absorbing asphalt and dark surfaces, significantly lowering ambient air temperatures. By providing direct solar protection for pedestrians and cyclists, it ensures safer and more comfortable outdoor movement during extreme heat events.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Prioritize planting in low-income neighborhoods with least canopy; involve communities in placement and stewardship to build local ownership and long-term tree survival.
Dependencies: Availability of suitable urban tree species adapted to local climate conditions, "Funding for tree procurement, planting, and long-term maintenance", "Technical expertise in urban forestry and street tree management", "Coordination with utility and infrastructure agencies to determine planting locations", "Community and stakeholder engagement for route selection and stewardship"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of street trees planted annually, "Increase in urban tree canopy coverage along cool corridors (%)", "Reduction in ambient temperature along planted corridors (°C)", "Increase in pedestrian and cyclist activity in shaded areas (%)", "Survival and establishment rate of planted trees (%)"
Further Resources: EPA (2023). Using Trees to Reduce Heat Islands. https://www.epa.gov/heatislands | Nowak, D.J. et al. (2022). Assessing urban forest effects. USDA Forest Service.

Action Name: Adopt Thermal Comfort Policies for Buildings and Public Spaces
Description: Adopt thermal comfort policies that set minimum indoor temperature standards in rental housing, workplaces, and public buildings, and require owners to provide adequate cooling to protect occupants from dangerous heat exposure.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Set minimum indoor temperature standards in rental housing and workplaces to protect low-income tenants and workers who cannot self-regulate their thermal environment.
Dependencies: Legislative authority to set minimum indoor thermal comfort standards, "Enforcement mechanisms and inspection capacity for rental housing and workplaces", "Technical guidance and support for building owners to achieve compliance", "Collaboration with housing, health, and labor regulatory authorities", "Monitoring systems to verify compliance and track temperature standards"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Percentage of rental housing meeting thermal comfort standards, "Number of workplace and building compliance inspections conducted", "Reduction in heat-related health incidents in monitored buildings", "Number of enforcement actions for non-compliant properties", "Proportion of public buildings meeting minimum temperature standards (%)"
Further Resources: ASHRAE (2022). Standard 55: Thermal Environmental Conditions for Human Occupancy. https://www.ashrae.org | WHO (2021). Housing and Health Guidelines. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241550376

Action Name: Launch Training and Upskilling Programs for Heat-Resilient Jobs
Description: Launch training and upskilling programs that equip workers with skills for heat-resilient jobs—including building retrofitting, green infrastructure maintenance, and emergency response—while creating green employment opportunities.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Partner with community organizations and educational institutions; target programs at underemployed and low-income residents to ensure heat-resilient jobs deliver economic equity.
Dependencies: Development of training curricula aligned with heat-resilient sector needs, "Collaboration with employers and industry associations for curriculum design", "Funding for training program delivery and participant support", "Accreditation and certification frameworks for new green skills", "Identification of priority sectors and current workforce skill gaps"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of workers trained in heat-resilient and green economy skills, "Number of green jobs created or filled through training programs", "Employment rate of program graduates within 12 months (%)", "Reduction in identified skill gaps for heat-resilient infrastructure roles", "Diversity and inclusion of underrepresented groups in training programs (%)"
Further Resources: ILO (2019). Working on a Warmer Planet. https://www.ilo.org | World Bank (2021). Jobs and Development. https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/jobsanddevelopment

Action Name: Develop Transit-Oriented Neighborhoods to Reduce Heat Exposure
Description: Develop transit-oriented neighborhoods that concentrate housing, services, and employment around transit hubs, reducing car dependency, outdoor heat exposure from long commutes, and the urban heat island effects of sprawl and parking lots.
Sector: Transportation; Buildings; Economic Development; City Administration
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: TOD must include affordable housing requirements near transit hubs to prevent displacement of low-income residents who benefit most from reduced car dependency.
Dependencies: Policy and regulatory support for transit-oriented development zoning, "Investment in transit infrastructure, frequency, and service quality", "Land-use planning and zoning reforms to enable mixed-use density near transit hubs", "Community engagement in transit-oriented neighborhood design", "Coordination between transport, housing, and urban planning departments"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Reduction in per capita vehicle kilometers traveled in transit-oriented neighborhoods, "Increase in public transit ridership in target neighborhoods (%)", "Percentage of residents within walking distance (500m) of transit hubs", "Reduction in urban heat island effect linked to reduced car dependency", "Decrease in commuting-related outdoor heat exposure"
Further Resources: ITDP (2017). TOD Standard. https://itdp.org/publication/tod-standard/ | IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch8 (2022). Urban Systems. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-8/

Action Name: Launch Tree Planting Campaigns on Public and Private Land
Description: Launch city-wide and community tree planting campaigns on public land, streets, parks, and through private property programs to rapidly expand urban tree canopy, reduce urban heat island intensity, and improve air quality and community wellbeing.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Prioritize low-income areas with least canopy; engage residents in design and maintenance to ensure long-term benefit and local ownership of green assets.
Dependencies: Availability of tree seedlings, planting materials, and species-appropriate stock, "Community volunteer mobilization and engagement capacity", "Coordination with private property owners for access to private land", "Funding for tree procurement, planting, and aftercare programs", "Collaboration with local government, schools, and environmental organizations"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of trees planted per year across public and private land, "Survival rate of planted trees after one and three years (%)", "Increase in urban tree canopy coverage (%)", "Number of community participants in tree planting campaigns", "Estimated reduction in urban heat island intensity from expanded canopy"
Further Resources: EPA (2023). Using Trees to Reduce Heat Islands. https://www.epa.gov/heatislands | Nowak, D.J. et al. (2022). Assessing urban forest effects. USDA Forest Service.

Action Name: Enforce Tree Protection Regulations in Urban Areas
Description: Enforce regulations protecting existing urban trees from removal, damage, and disease, maintaining established tree canopy that provides immediate and ongoing cooling, air quality, and biodiversity benefits.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Apply citywide with prioritized enforcement in low-income neighborhoods, where trees provide critical cooling but face higher removal pressure from development.
Dependencies: Clear legal framework for tree protection with defined penalties for violations, "Adequate enforcement and inspection capacity with trained officers", "Urban tree inventory and mapping systems to identify protected trees", "Public awareness campaigns on tree protection regulations and reporting violations", "Remediation requirements and processes for trees damaged or removed illegally"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Reduction in unauthorized tree removal incidents per year, "Percentage of urban trees covered by legal protection orders", "Number of enforcement actions taken annually for tree protection violations", "Net change in urban tree canopy coverage attributed to protection measures", "Compliance rate with tree protection regulations among developers and property owners (%)"
Further Resources: EPA (2023). Using Trees to Reduce Heat Islands. https://www.epa.gov/heatislands | Nowak, D.J. et al. (2022). Assessing urban forest effects. USDA Forest Service.

Action Name: Develop an Urban Forestry Plan
Description: Develop a comprehensive urban forestry plan that sets targets for canopy coverage, defines species selection criteria, maps priority planting areas, and establishes maintenance protocols to grow and sustain a resilient urban forest.
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Plans must target equitable canopy distribution, prioritizing low-income neighborhoods with least tree cover; include communities in species selection and stewardship planning.
Dependencies: Cross-departmental collaboration and governance structure for plan development, "Community and stakeholder consultation to define priorities and targets", "Comprehensive urban tree canopy inventory and mapping data", "Dedicated funding and implementation resources for plan delivery", "Integration with urban planning, biodiversity, and climate resilience frameworks"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Percentage of citywide tree canopy coverage target achieved, "Number of priority planting areas identified and addressed per year", "Annual tree planting targets met as proportion of plan goals (%)", "Increase in urban tree species diversity index", "Reduction in urban heat island intensity attributed to urban forestry plan implementation"
Further Resources: USDA Forest Service (2022). Urban and Community Forestry Program. https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/urban-forests | EPA (2023). Using Trees to Reduce Heat Islands. https://www.epa.gov/heatislands

Action Name: Launch Wellness Check Programs for Heat-Vulnerable Populations
Description: Launch wellness check programs that regularly contact and visit heat-vulnerable residents—including elderly people living alone, people with chronic illness, and those without home cooling—during heatwaves to ensure their safety and connect them with services.
Sector: Disaster Risk Management; Public Health; Informal Settlements
Equity and Inclusion Considerations: Annually update participant lists with community organization support to reach isolated elderly, low-income, and disabled residents at greatest risk during heat events.
Dependencies: Registry or identification system for heat-vulnerable residents requiring outreach, "Volunteer and community health worker networks for check delivery", "Coordination with health services, social services, and emergency agencies", "Communication protocols and safety guidelines for wellness check visits and calls", "Funding for program staffing and operations during heat season"
Potential Key Performance Indicators: Number of individuals reached through wellness check programs during heat events, "Frequency of wellness checks conducted per heat-vulnerable resident", "Reduction in heat-related hospitalizations among target populations", "Number of referrals to health services and cooling centers made through program", "Coverage rate of identified heat-vulnerable population reached by program (%)"
Further Resources: CDC (2023). Wellness Checks for Extreme Heat. https://www.cdc.gov | WHO (2021). Heat-Health Action Plans. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240008410
